Threat.value: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: I have to be on guard all the time
If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

issues.item: Triggers: Being Praised: Receiving praise or positive attention
issues.explanation: 'Being praised' is a hard-to-explain trigger in a profile otherwise centered on a life-threatening accident with sensory trigger cues, intrusive reliving, and hypervigilant threat monitoring. Unlike smell or darkness, praise has no evident link to the accident-based memory/threat pattern and stands out as clinically incoherent unless additional interpersonal trauma context were present.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: 'Institutional failure' fits betrayal, assault, military, or disaster-response contexts more naturally than a single life-threatening accident in a financial analyst. In this profile the other appraisals focus on danger and inability to cope; this item introduces a qualitatively different blame/betrayal theme that is not supported by the trauma type, trigger pattern, or memory content.

vignette: John, a 63-year-old Oceania male and financial analyst, has been struggling with the aftermath of a life-threatening accident that occurred six months ago. The trauma left deep psychological scars, which have significantly affected his daily functioning and personal relationships. John's wife had noticed changes in him almost immediately after the incident, but he didn't seek help until recently. The traumatic event involved a near-fatal car crash on a dark highway. As John was driving home late one night, he suddenly heard screeching tires and a loud bang as his vehicle collided with another car that had veered into his lane. The smell of burning rubber and the sound of shattering glass filled the air. He remembers the darkness overwhelming him as everything went silent, followed by an intense feeling of fear and helplessness. Since the accident, John has found himself reacting strongly to related triggers. The smell of burnt rubber or car exhaust can instantly transport him back to that moment, making it feel like the event is happening again rather than something from the past. He often hears the screeching tires in his head as if he were right there. Dark spaces and the sounds of cars passing by can trigger vivid recollections of the accident, causing intense distress. John had come to believe that he needs to be on guard all the time because you never know what can happen next. This hypervigilance has led him to constantly scan for exits whenever he enters a room or building. He wakes up in the middle of the night to check if everything is safe, certain that his body reacts to danger before he even has time to think. The combination of these triggers and negative appraisals has created a self-reinforcing cycle. When John encounters a trigger, such as the smell of burnt rubber while refueling at a gas station or hearing car sounds in the neighborhood, it immediately brings back the memory of the accident. This often leaves him feeling like he is reliving the trauma right then and there. His negative appraisals reinforce his threat perceptions. He fears that if he thinks about the event too much, he will not be able to handle it, which leads him to avoid situations where triggers might occur. For instance, John started avoiding driving at night altogether, a significant change given how often this was part of his work routine as a financial analyst who frequently traveled to evening meetings. John's hypervigilance has also affected his daily life in profound ways. He finds it hard to relax and enjoy activities because he is always scanning for potential threats. This constant state of alertness has taken a toll on both his physical health, leading to insomnia and fatigue, and his emotional well-being, causing him to feel isolated from others. What frightens John most is the unpredictability of when these memories might intrude into his consciousness without warning. He feels as though he can never truly be at peace because the memory lingers, always ready to surface. His fear of triggers has also led him to avoid certain places and activities that once brought him joy. The constant vigilance and avoidance behaviors have strained John's relationship with his wife. She notices how distant and anxious he becomes when out in public or driving. He avoids going on vacations they had planned, and this avoidance has led to feelings of frustration and misunderstanding between them. John finally sought help because the burden of these symptoms became too overwhelming for him to manage alone. He is most hoping for a way to regain control over his life and find peace from the constant fear that haunts him. He wants to be able to drive again without feeling like he's on edge, to enjoy dark spaces and car sounds without them bringing back the traumatic memories. Most importantly, John hopes to feel safe in his daily life once more.
